summary: Reviewed the dvpwa aiohttp application (the `sqli` package: views, routes, middlewares, DAO layer, auth utils, jinja2 setup, schema/config, and templates) plus deployment config. This is an intentionally vulnerable teaching app, and the code confirms it: a classic unauthenticated SQL injection in the student-creation query, application-wide disabling of Jinja2 autoescaping leading to stored XSS, MD5 password hashing, globally disabled CSRF protection, non-HttpOnly session cookies, aiohttp debug mode enabled, and missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (notably the admin-only evaluate route). Overall risk is critical: several issues are directly and remotely exploitable by unauthenticated users. Static asset JS libraries were not audited.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement by Python %-formatting the raw `name` value directly into the SQL string instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The value flows from the unauthenticated POST /students/ handler (views.students, views.py:54-57) which reads data['name'] straight from request.post() with no validation. An attacker can submit a name like `x'); DROP TABLE marks; --` or use it for boolean/stacked queries to read or destroy arbitrary data. No authentication is required to reach this sink. All other DAO methods (course/review/mark/user, and Student.get/get_many) correctly use bound parameters; this is the one that concatenates.
findings.evidence:
views.py:55-57: `data = await request.post(); ... await Student.create(conn, data['name'])`.
student.py:41-45: `q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})` then `await cur.execute(q)` with the pre-formatted string and no params.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: `await cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name})` and never build SQL with %-formatting or f-strings. Also validate input with STUDENT_SCHEMA.

findings.title: Stored/reflected XSS from application-wide autoescape=False in Jinja2
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so every template renders variables as raw HTML unless a filter is applied. User-controlled values are then emitted unescaped: course review_text (course.jinja2:22), course.title/description (course.jinja2:14-15, student.jinja2:19-20), and student name (students.jinja2:16). The clearest vector is stored XSS via reviews: an unauthenticated user POSTs a review to /courses/{id}/review (views.review, views.py:129) containing `<script>...</script>`, which is stored and then rendered raw to every visitor of the course page. Because session cookies are not HttpOnly, this escalates to session/account theft.
findings.evidence:
app.py:33-35: `setup_jinja(app, loader=..., context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)`.
course.jinja2:22: `{{ review.review_text }}` (no `| e`).
review_text source: views.py:120-129 reads data.get('review_text') from POST and stores it via Review.create unauthenticated.
findings.recommendation: Enable autoescaping (autoescape=True, the aiohttp_jinja2 default) and remove now-redundant manual `| e` filters, or explicitly mark trusted content only. Never disable autoescape globally.

findings.title: Missing authorization on admin-only evaluate endpoint (and other state-changing routes)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns marks to students but has no authentication/authorization check. The UI only exposes the evaluate form to admins (course.jinja2:41 `{% if auth_user.is_admin %}`), showing the operation is intended to be admin-only, yet the route POST /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id} (routes.py:21-23) invokes the handler with no @authorize(ensure_admin=True). Any unauthenticated client can POST points and forge grades. The same missing-guard pattern also affects student creation (views.students, views.py:54-57), course creation (views.courses, views.py:86-90) and review creation (views.review) — none require authentication despite templates gating the forms behind login. The authorize() decorator exists (utils/auth.py:12) but is only applied to logout.
findings.evidence: routes.py:22-23 registers views.evaluate with no auth wrapper; views.py:134-153 has no get_auth_user/authorize call. Contrast logout at views.py:156 which uses @authorize(). Template gate at course.jinja2:41 confirms admin-only intent.
findings.recommendation: Apply @authorize(ensure_admin=True) to evaluate and @authorize() to the other state-changing handlers (student/course/review creation), enforcing checks server-side rather than relying on template conditionals.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled globally
findings.description: A working CSRF middleware exists (middlewares.py:25-38) and templates render `_csrf_token` hidden fields, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no CSRF validation ever runs. Every state-changing POST (login, student/course/review creation, evaluate, logout) is therefore vulnerable to cross-site request forgery: an attacker's page can auto-submit forms to these endpoints using the victim's session cookie. Combined with the missing per-handler auth, an attacker can, for example, force a logged-in admin's browser to create grades or content.
findings.evidence: app.py:25-30 middlewares=[session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware] — csrf_middleware is commented out. middlewares.py:26-38 defines a functional csrf_middleware that is never registered.
findings.recommendation: Add csrf_middleware to the middlewares list so the existing token check runs on all POST requests.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5
findings.description: Password verification compares the stored hash to a plain, unsalted MD5 of the submitted password. MD5 is a fast, broken hash unsuitable for passwords: if the users table is disclosed (e.g., via the SQL injection above), the hashes are trivially cracked with rainbow tables/GPU brute force, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. The comparison is also non-constant-time.
findings.evidence: user.py:1 `from hashlib import md5`; user.py:41 `return self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()`. Called from views.py:41 during login.
findings.recommendation: Use a purpose-built password KDF (bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2) with a per-user salt, and compare using a constant-time function. Rehash existing passwords on next login.

findings.title: Session cookie not marked HttpOnly
findings.description: The Redis-backed session storage is created with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Given the stored XSS enabled by autoescape=False, an attacker's injected script can exfiltrate the session cookie via document.cookie and hijack the victim's authenticated session, including an admin's.
findings.recommendation: Set httponly=True (the default) and also set secure=True and an appropriate SameSite attribute for session cookies.

findings.title: aiohttp application debug mode enabled
findings.description: The Application is constructed with debug=True unconditionally, regardless of environment. Debug mode enables extra diagnostics and more verbose error behavior that can leak internal details and increase attack surface if this configuration is used in production. It should be driven by configuration rather than hardcoded on.
findings.recommendation: Drive debug from configuration/environment and default it to False for production deployments.
